title: The ecliptic and the zodiac
subtitle: The one line in the sky that the Sun, Moon and planets all follow

sections.heading: The Sun's yearly path
body: After this lesson you will be able to trace the ecliptic across your own sky on any night, name the constellations along it, and explain why the summer Sun is high and the winter Sun low.

Earth circles the Sun once a year. From our moving platform the Sun seems to drift eastward against the background stars, about 1° a day, and returns to its starting point after a year. The line it follows is called the ecliptic. It is simply the plane of Earth's orbit drawn on the sky. You cannot see the stars behind the Sun, but you can work out where it is, and astronomers have tracked it for thousands of years.

The constellations the ecliptic passes through are the zodiac. By the official boundaries drawn by the International Astronomical Union in 1930 there are thirteen: Pisces, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpius, Ophiuchus, Sagittarius, Capricornus and Aquarius. The Sun spends very unequal times in them: about six weeks in sprawling Virgo, under a week in Scorpius, and nearly three weeks in Ophiuchus, which tradition leaves out.

steps.caption: A star chart with daylight removed. The dots show the Sun every 15 days from the March equinox (right) to the September equinox (left), sliding east through Pisces, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer and Leo. The line it follows is the ecliptic.

The thirteenth zodiac constellation. In 2027 the Sun crosses a corner of Scorpius from November 24 to 30, then spends November 30 to December 19 inside Ophiuchus before entering Sagittarius. The dots are five days apart.

figures.caption: As Earth goes round the Sun, the Sun appears in front of a different zodiac constellation, one after another, and the constellation on the opposite side is the one up at midnight. Press Play a year and watch the amber line sweep the whole ring once a year; notice how small Scorpius's share of the ring is.

check.prompt: On December 10 the Sun is in front of Ophiuchus. Which zodiac constellation is high in the sky around midnight?
choices: Taurus
Ophiuchus
Scorpius
Virgo
check.explanation: At midnight you face directly away from the Sun, so you see the zodiac constellation on the far side of the ring: Taurus. Ophiuchus itself is hidden in daylight.

sections.heading: Constellations and signs
body: The twelve signs of astrology share their names with zodiac constellations but are not the same thing. A sign is one of twelve equal 30° slices of the ecliptic, counted from the point where the Sun stands at the March equinox. A constellation is a patch of sky of irregular size with fixed boundaries among the stars.

When the signs were laid out, more than two thousand years ago, each roughly matched its constellation. Since then a slow wobble of Earth's axis, called precession, has shifted the equinox point westward by about one whole constellation. So on a date when the sign in a horoscope column is Aries, the Sun is actually in front of the stars of Pisces. In this course, names always mean the constellations.

figures.caption: Signs are equal 30° slices counted from the March equinox point; constellations are star patterns of every width. Precession has slid the equinox point about 28° west in 2,000 years, so today the signs sit almost a whole constellation off the stars. Switch to 2,000 years ago to see them line up.

misconception.myth: Your star sign is the constellation the Sun was in front of on the day you were born.
misconception.fact: For most birthdays the Sun was in front of the constellation to the west of your sign, because precession has slid the signs almost a whole constellation since they were laid out. About 1 person in 20 was born with the Sun in Ophiuchus, which has no sign at all.

sections.heading: A tilted path
body: Earth's axis is tilted 23.4° to its orbit, so the ecliptic is tilted 23.4° to the celestial equator. For half the year the Sun is north of the equator and for half it is south. Around June 21 it is at its farthest north: from Brooklyn it climbs 73° high at midday and stays up for 15 hours. Around December 21 it is at its farthest south, only 26° up at noon, and the day lasts barely 9 hours. That difference in the height of the Sun and the length of the day, and not any change in distance, is what makes the seasons.

At night the picture reverses. The part of the ecliptic that is up at midnight is the part opposite the Sun. A full Moon is opposite the Sun too, so the full Moons of winter ride high overhead, where the summer Sun was, and the full Moons of summer skim low across the south. Planets follow the same rule: one that is opposite the Sun in winter is high, in summer low.

steps.caption: Facing south at midday on June 21. Three daily arcs of the Sun, marked every hour: the top one is today, the middle one the March equinox, the bottom one December 21. At noon the Sun stands 73°, 49° and 26° high.
Midnight under the full Moon of December 13, 2027. The Moon is 75° up, almost overhead, on the stretch of the ecliptic where the June Sun stands.
The full Moon of June 18–19, 2027 at 1 am, as high as it gets: 22°, about two fists. It follows the low path of the winter Sun.

figures.caption: Earth's axis stays tilted the same way in space all year. Around the June solstice the northern half leans toward the Sun, and around the December solstice the southern half does: the Sun climbs higher and stays up longer there, and its light falls more directly. The figure uses your location; slide to January and notice that Earth is then at its closest to the Sun.

misconception.myth: It is summer when Earth is closest to the Sun and winter when it is farthest.
misconception.fact: Earth's distance from the Sun changes by only about 3% in a year, and Earth is closest in early January, during the northern winter. The seasons come from the tilt: it changes how high the Sun climbs and how long it stays up, and that is also why the two hemispheres have opposite seasons.

thinkAbout.question: If the seasons really came from changing distance, what would be true of Australia's seasons compared with Canada's?
thinkAbout.answer: Both countries would have summer at the same time, when the whole Earth was nearest the Sun. In fact Australia has summer in December and January, exactly when Canada has winter. Only the tilt explains that: when one hemisphere leans toward the Sun, the other leans away.

sections.tryIt: Tonight, find the Moon or any bright planet and one other of them, or a zodiac star such as Aldebaran, Regulus, Spica or Antares. Sweep your arm from one to the other and on across the sky. That arc is the ecliptic: the Sun was on it today.

keyPoints: The ecliptic is the Sun's yearly path among the stars: the plane of Earth's orbit seen from inside.
Thirteen constellations lie on it, including Ophiuchus; the twelve astrological signs are equal 30° slices that no longer line up with the constellations.
The ecliptic is tilted 23.4° to the celestial equator, which gives the high summer Sun, the low winter Sun and the seasons.
At night the ecliptic does the opposite of the daytime Sun: high on winter nights, low on summer nights.

choices: The path the Moon's shadow traces on Earth
The Sun's apparent yearly path among the stars
The line of the horizon at sunset
The band of the Milky Way
questions.explanation: The ecliptic is the plane of Earth's orbit projected on the sky, which is where the Sun appears from Earth over a year.

questions.prompt: Which constellation does the Sun pass through that is not one of the twelve traditional zodiac figures?
choices: Orion
Cetus
Ophiuchus
Auriga
questions.explanation: By the modern boundaries the Sun spends nearly three weeks in Ophiuchus, between Scorpius and Sagittarius.

questions.prompt: Why is the full Moon so high in the sky in December?
choices: The Moon is closer to Earth in winter
Cold air bends its light upward
The Moon's orbit tilts by 23° in winter
A full Moon is opposite the Sun, so it sits on the part of the ecliptic where the summer Sun stands
questions.explanation: When the Sun is at the low, southern end of the ecliptic, the point opposite it, where a full Moon must be, is at the high, northern end.

questions.prompt: How does an astrological sign differ from a zodiac constellation?
choices: A sign is an equal 30° slice of the ecliptic measured from the equinox; a constellation is a patch of stars of irregular size
They are two names for the same thing
A sign is larger than a constellation
Signs are in the northern sky, constellations in the southern
questions.explanation: Precession has slid the equal signs about one constellation west of the star patterns they were named for.

choices: Earth is closer to the Sun in summer
The Sun gives off more heat in summer
Earth's axis is tilted 23.4°, changing the height of the Sun and the length of the day
The Moon blocks sunlight in winter
questions.explanation: The tilt puts the Sun high and the days long in summer, low and short in winter. Earth is in fact closest to the Sun in early January.
